0:35:02 — Robotics, ChatGPT, and What Comes Next

Why robotics is an imperative

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: I’m curious how you think about robotics. Like you mentioned earlier, at some point if we had automated labor in the same way we’re going to have automated intelligence, things might get even crazier. The labor market is much bigger in the white collar market.

Sam Altman: If we don’t have it, then things get really crazy. If the role for people in the world is to be like the actuators of AI in the cloud —

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Bad.

Sam Altman: Very bad. Very bad. So I think it’s like much crazier if we don’t get it than we do.

A ChatGPT moment for robots in two or three years

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: It’s an imperative. Help me understand your sense of progress in that. Because unlike in AI, where everyone is now kind of on the same page of like it’s going fast — you can find extremely smart people that say it’s like end of this year, and you can find extremely smart people that say it’s 20 years from now or something.

Sam Altman: It’s not 20 years. I would say we get the ChatGPT moment for robotics in the next like two or three years.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: What would that be like? Do you know what that is?

Sam Altman: Something where most people have like a real wow. Not like, I saw this video of a robot dog doing something crazy, but I was somehow able to convince myself that a really important thing happened. One of the things about the ChatGPT moment was that you could just go use it.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Yeah.

Sam Altman: Like, I didn’t have to believe someone who said AI is coming soon. You could just go try it.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Yeah.

Sam Altman: And if you can go like, you know, type in a command and a robot can do something crazy, and you can like watch it even if you’re not physically there — I think that would have the same kind of like, whoa, it just did this thing.

How ChatGPT actually shipped: the playground, GPT-3.5, and a rename hours before launch

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Wasn’t ChatGPT like not this monolithic goal, but sort of like a side experiment that you decided to release? Can you tell that story? May be instructive for something similar happening in robotics. Everyone seems to want to fold laundry, but maybe it’s something very different.

Sam Altman: When we launched GPT-3, we’re trying to make money, trying to get people to use this API.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Yeah.

Sam Altman: And the only commercial use case that was really working — the model was just so dumb. Like, if you went back and used it you’d be astonished. The only commercial use case that was working was copywriting, you know. So you pay like some marketing firm 20 bucks, and they paid us 20 cents for the AI to like write you a landing page or whatever.

But in addition to that one commercial use case, developers were using this thing we called the playground, which was like a testing interface to chat with the model. And it was really hard to do, because we had not tuned the model to be good to chat with. So you had to like give it a few examples of what it means to chat and then do it. But people really liked it. And I had learned this great lesson from YC [Y Combinator]: if you notice your users doing something, like, go down that path.

And so we decided that we would build a good chatbot, since that’s what people were doing. We started working on that, and we finished GPT-4 and we started using that internally. Like, this is a big deal. And we kind of thought that, all right, this is going to be a real update to the world about AI. And there’s a bunch of hard questions here about, you know, is this going to create a bunch of fake news, is going to say really offensive things, we’re going to get in trouble. So we decided we would start with a weaker version. The chat interface and GPT-4 at the same time seemed like a lot, so we would roll out the chat interface and GPT-3.5.

In fact, it was originally going to be called Chat with GPT-3.5. And we didn’t plan to be product. Didn’t think it’d be a huge hit, but did think it would get the world to like catch up with this and realize something was going on. And we mercifully renamed it ChatGPT a few hours before launch and put it out as like a research preview.

And the thought was we’d put it out as a research preview, and then a few months later we would launch a product with GPT-4. And for whatever reason, that model was over the threshold where, even though we had gotten used to it internally, people said, “Okay, this is awesome.” There maybe wasn’t that much utility yet, but it was an incredible moment for people to feel AI progress and use something that they enjoyed using. And then by the time we put GPT-4, something they really got benefit out of using too.

Why chat stayed the interface

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Are you surprised that that remains kind of the intuitive interface between us and this alien intelligence, even including coding? Like, mostly that’s me talking to the computer telling it what to build.

Sam Altman: No, because I’m like a massive texter.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Yeah.

Sam Altman: I’ve been a massive texter my whole life. I think part of my own insight of why that was a good interface is I’m like, I know how to do this. I know what it’s like to just like start chatting in a text box.

Diffusion, marketing, and a product that markets itself

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Any other thoughts on this notion of diffusion and how to make it faster? Like, if the mission is get intelligence into the hands and more useful for everyone, a key part of that is like, I don’t know, a marketing campaign or something. Like, how do you get this to diffuse faster than it seems to be doing naturally to me?

Sam Altman: I think the key thing is just make it better. Like, I kind of believe that a truly great product markets itself. There was no ChatGPT marketing campaign at the beginning.

And I think as we get to this next stage of models, and we figure out how to make products that are as great as the models themselves, there will be such incredible utility that people will spread it very quickly. We should definitely do more marketing — like, the AI is not too popular for as much as people use it, or they have very understandable anxiety about where it can go. And so that kind of stuff, I think some great marketing would be helpful for. But in terms of value people are getting out of their products, and getting their products to grow: faster models, more compute, better products. That will do it.

Recruiting researchers with a heretical belief

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: There was this period where the recruiting of researchers, the retention of them, the incentivizing of them, was like the defining story in the competitive landscape or whatever. I think there’s lots of stories about you successfully recruiting great researchers, and there’s been many that have come through OpenAI and had huge impacts. Some of which are known, some of which are lesser-known names. I’m just curious about this whole genre of like what you learned about how to recruit this class of person. What matters to them, and how you did it. I’ve never heard you talk about like the actual tactical moves you pulled to recruit somebody in the early days.

Sam Altman: I think it was quite simple, which was that we believed that AGI was possible and it was worth going after, and we’re willing to say that. And that was like an insane, heretical belief.

When we first announced OpenAI, all of these, like, you know, giants of the field, these experts, were saying this is like insane. It’s hypy. It’s irresponsible. Really respected people like Yann LeCun or whatever telling journalists like, oh, these guys aren’t very good and it’s not going to work. But the fact that we were able to say we’re gonna go for this — it really appealed to a certain kind of researcher that also wanted to like go on this crazy adventure with low probability of success. And an ambitious, kind of audacious vision is a very powerful recruiting tool.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Yeah. You think — you’ve written that it’s actually easier sometimes to build things that are harder, because of this reason.

Sam Altman: I super believe in this. It’s one of my most frequent pieces of advice to YC founders, and I tried to really live it at OpenAI. Just do something harder. Do something that matters. Like, do something that is important, and if you don’t do it, if your company doesn’t succeed, might not happen.

Investors who actually show up

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: You were an investor, and our investor. You’ve done a lot of it, and at one point that’s what you did. What have you learned about investors being on the other side?

Sam Altman: The number of investors that actually show up and try to help you is unbelievably small. Josh Kushner, absolute MVP investor, unbelievable, has like worked around the clock for what feels like years to help us. He is the only investor that I could point to that is proactively incredibly helpful all the time. There are more people that could do that.

And there are many other investors that have also been helpful, and that have great strategic advice, and that do things when, you know, we ask them to do it. But the like constant, just relentless all-in support is surprisingly rare from investors. Maybe I’m biased cuz I always liked it when people said that about me. But I think founders really love that, and it actually like moves the needle. And as an investor, it’s the most fun way to do —

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Me and my friend play this game where we text each other all the time, and the prompt of the text is something I don’t want you to know about me.

Sam Altman: I’m tired. I don’t think I’m supposed — I’ve been doing this a long time. It’s tiring.

0:44:39 — The Weight of Leading OpenAI

“I’m tired”

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: How do you get through that?

Sam Altman: Just keep going.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: It begs the question, like, is there amount of being tired that would make you stop doing this?

Sam Altman: No, no, no. I mean, this is the coolest job in the world. I plan to do this for the rest of my career. But it’s like much harder than I have a way to explain to people. I feel very grateful to get to do this. This is not me complaining.

Month 24 after superintelligence: not very much

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: What’s coming next? Like, we talked about automated AI researchers that next year, the year after. Like, how do you think about what is happening in the next 6 to 36 months? Maybe that’s too far out to forecast in this crazy exponential. Maybe a different version of the question is like, let’s say in, you know, month 23 from now we have something that everybody agrees is super intelligence. What happens in month 24?

Sam Altman: And my answer would be, not very much. The kind of like cult worship of the machine god states — those people believe that like more is going to happen quickly than is going to happen. Eventually a lot will happen. But eventually a lot was going to happen anyway.

Like the rate of human progress, and you know how different each decade is going to be, and how much each decade is more different than the decade from before. That’s been happening for a long time — obviously ups and downs, but directionally.

And I think the right way to think about this: everybody wants to be the hero of the story, everybody wants to feel like they were there for the moment of the machine god and they played some crazy role. But you know, this is another step, and it was hard to imagine 50 years ago, and the step 50 years from now is hard to imagine today. And I think the right mental framework is just to zoom way out, and it’s a pretty smooth exponential.

Codex, moats, and what stays scarce when intelligence is a commodity

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Tell me a little bit about the experience of watching Codex take off, and how much that is tied to what I would describe as like a competitive advantage of distribution that you built through chat. And this is a gateway into a question about like moats in general in AI — like, what you think will drive real competitive advantage in the business over time.

Sam Altman: I think Codex mostly is winning because it’s the best product and the best model. We do get some advantage from ChatGPT bundling, but very very tiny. That is mostly not what it’s been about.

It has made me reflect a lot on this question of competitive advantage. Because, you know, like, brilliant intelligence can migrate from any product to any other product. And network effects still have a competitive advantage.

Economic scale and the ability to like make the cheapest compute fleets, whatever, still have a competitive advantage. But the product advantage — like, if we could get people to move over to Codex, and someone builds something better, they can get people to move from Codex. So it has made me reflect on that a lot.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: There’s a really interesting question about whether this is going in the direction of a commodity. Like, is intelligence going to be a pure fungible commodity, like rated oil [unclear in the audio; a second ASR pass heard “rate of the oil”] or something?

Sam Altman: Intelligence itself, I would say yes.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: So what is not going to be?

Sam Altman: Compute fleet, you know, like the scale of the compute fleet, the ability to make more compute. I think that’s like a very durable advantage, even if the product itself is not, because, you know, Codex can write any piece of software you want. The workflows, the integrations, the sort of like complex processes, the ability for teams to collaborate together — that stuff is all pretty powerful. Even like brand preference and familiarity is pretty powerful.

New hardware for an always-on assistant

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: How excited are you about new — obviously you’ve done interesting stuff in hardware that I’m sure you’ll announce later this year. How does that experiment feel and align with this sort of consumer distribution that you have?

Sam Altman: One of the reasons I’m interested in new hardware is, we were talking earlier about how a very powerful thing with AI is that it can be always on and proactive and just understand all your context. But current hardware is not good for that.

Like, we are working inside of a hardware paradigm that is 50 years old, something like that. And computers are amazing. Keyboard and mice, monitor. It’s an amazing thing. But like, we have to shape AI into that. And I’m excited to think about — I would love AI to be able to reference this conversation, but not so much that I’m willing to like crack my laptop open, put it here, and have it looking at you and listening to us while it’s going. But I would like a piece of hardware that socially was acceptable to do that, and also felt like it was designed for that kind of a thing.

Cognitive atrophy as the under-discussed question

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: As you think about the open questions — what debates in your own head, with your friends, with your colleagues here — what are the most interesting open debates or open questions that you don’t feel certain about but feel important?

Sam Altman: One that I don’t think gets much attention is, how are we going to avoid cognitive atrophy? How are we going to use these tools and make sure that we are like stretching our brains more and more, and continuing to understand the stuff that really matters?

There’s lots of versions of this that don’t — like, I remember when I was in school, I had this professor tell me like, you got to understand compilers. If you don’t, you will never be able to be a good programmer. Somehow that wasn’t quite right. But understanding at a reasonable level like how the major components of a computer system work has been important to me.

What oversupply of compute would look like

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Forced to imagine a scenario where we are somehow oversupplied in compute in 2 years time. What would be that story?

Sam Altman: It does feel possible. If the models get so smart and so efficient that they can kind of do everything we need, and, you know, build every piece of software we want — and if the bounds of our attention are such that they just cannot absorb more than what it turns out a fairly limited amount of compute can do — then we can get into oversupply. Also, if we don’t drive the cost curve down because we hit some sort of scaling wall, we could also get into oversupply. Like, the observation about uncapped demand implies a certain price.

Scaling laws, “the most hated prediction of all time”

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Can you give your point of view on scaling laws [3] today?

Sam Altman: Looking great.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Just looking good.

Sam Altman: In some sense, scaling laws are like the most hated prediction of all time. Everybody always wants to say a run can’t be like this, and yet it keeps going.

Alec Radford

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Who are your favorite unsung heroes in this company’s story?

Sam Altman: First person that came to mind is Alec Radford. Alec Radford is probably the most important not-very-well-known researcher in the whole history of the field, and also just a wonderful, like, top tier human being. He did the work that really became the GPT series, among many other important things.

But he also is someone who inspired, guided, nudged people in many other directions that turned out to be super important. And the thing I think is cool about him is, if you talk to people that worked with him, they will of course say, you know, generational genius, brilliant, innovative thinker, just so deep in his understanding and his work. But everybody will tell you, before they finish their statement, that just like, one of the nicest, most positive, best people they’ve ever interacted with.

Note

Editor’s note. Radford is the first author on the two reports that started the series, “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training” (2018) and “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners” (2019), and on CLIP [4] and Whisper [5]. He left OpenAI in 2025 to do independent research.

0:51:36 — OpenAI’s Biggest Lessons

The mistake: innovating on corporate structure

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: I love formative moments. And so as we wind up here, I’m curious to ask one of each. If you think about the whole OpenAI experience, what moment or chapter or whatever are you most proud of? Start with the other one, which is: what was like the most instructive thing that maybe you got wrong or did wrong or what have you, and what was it like to learn from it?

Sam Altman: I mean, a lot of things have gone wrong. A formative one that went wrong, which I haven’t talked about much, is we made a mistake to try to innovate in our structure in the beginning. We had a very good reason for it, which is we didn’t know how we were ever going to make money, and we really at the time weren’t sure at all what we’re going to look like when we grew up.

And of course we care about our mission, and we wanted to be structured in a way where even if the technology went on a very fast takeoff our mission was protected. And so we had this, like, you know, nonprofit structure. But I definitely learned something about why people don’t do that much. We would have saved ourselves a great deal of pain in many ways if we had not tried to innovate on our structure, and found some other way to preserve the central importance of the mission.

Maybe there was no other way. Maybe there was, for what we were doing and kind of the importance of it, nothing other than an exotic structure we could have come up with. I really learned over the last decade a big lesson about why people don’t usually do that.

Immunity to other people’s opinions

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: Is there anything else formative of your life that makes you you that we didn’t talk about? This is like the question that’s always the most interesting to me.

Sam Altman: Becoming relatively immune to people having strong opinions about me — that I think I developed later in life, as like realizing that, man, just, if you’re going to be at the center of like this crazy revolution, everybody’s going to project a lot of stuff onto you, and you got to just quickly learn to make peace about that.

I think there were also things I learned later in life about like how to be very calm and not anxious really about stuff. In terms of what drives me and what I care about, and kind of like how I want to live my life on the whole, I felt like, you know, for whatever reason, the like 10-year-old version of me was pretty fully formed. I think I just kind of came out this way.

What he’s proudest of

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: How about the thing you’re proud of looking back on?

Sam Altman: I’m most proud of how many times we were right when the rest of the world was wrong, in an important way that put the world on a trajectory now that I’m very proud to have played a role in. That feels awesome. And then also, like, for all the crap that’s happened, like the spiritual growth or whatever you want to call it that I’ve gotten to have, of like learning just incredible resilience and what that does for making me happy in the rest of my life. Yeah, very grateful for that.

The kindest thing

Patrick O’Shaughnessy: When I do these, I ask everyone the same traditional closing question. What is the kindest thing that anyone’s ever done for you?

Sam Altman: I feel incredibly lucky about how many people have gone way out of their way to be very kind to me throughout my entire life. As I’m thinking of this, there’s just this like montage of moments from life where people have been unbelievably nice to me. Yesterday, my kid shared his blueberries with me for the first time. That was very sweet.

References

Talk and source

  • YouTube video (~56 min; Invest Like The Best, published July 28, 2026)
  • Invest Like The Best — the show, from Colossus

People

  • Sam Altman — cofounder and CEO, OpenAI
  • Patrick O’Shaughnessy — host, Invest Like The Best; CEO of Positive Sum
  • Alec Radford, Yann LeCun, Dario Amodei, Peter Thiel, Paul Graham, Josh Kushner

Companies and products

  • OpenAI — ChatGPT, Codex, GPT-4, Jalapeño
  • Microsoft, Oracle, Nvidia, Broadcom, Y Combinator
  • Hugging Face, Moonshot AI (Kimi), DeepSeek

Concepts and background

  • Artificial general intelligence, technological singularity, recursive self-improvement
  • Knowledge distillation, Pareto efficiency, optical computing, network effects
  • Zero-day vulnerability, regulatory capture, data center cooling

Papers and technical reports

  1. Brown, T., Mann, B., Ryder, N., et al. “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.” NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv:2005.14165), May 28, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165
  2. Wang, Z., Shi, T., He, J., Cai, M., Zhang, J., Song, D. “CyberGym: Evaluating AI Agents’ Real-World Cybersecurity Capabilities at Scale.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2506.02548), June 3, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02548
  3. Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., Henighan, T., et al. “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2001.08361), January 23, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361
  4. Radford, A., Kim, J. W., Hallacy, C., et al. “Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision.” ICML 2021 (arXiv:2103.00020), February 26, 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020
  5. Radford, A., Kim, J. W., Xu, T., Brockman, G., McLeavey, C., Sutskever, I. “Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision.” ICML 2023 (arXiv:2212.04356), December 6, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356

Related Posts

  • Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: Hugging Face’s forensic account of the incident Altman describes here in two sentences, including the evaluation settings his telling leaves out.
  • Greg Brockman on the Founding of OpenAI and the 72 Hours That Nearly Ended It: the same decade told by the cofounder, with the compute-conviction story dated differently and the nonprofit structure defended rather than regretted.
  • Karen Hao on Empire of AI: OpenAI, AGI Believers, and a New Colonialism: a hostile outside reading of the concentration-of-power argument Altman makes here, which casts OpenAI as one of the concentrators.
  • Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away: the timeline counterweight to “very close, like not that much longer,” from someone who watched the same models from inside.
  • When AI Builds Itself: the mapped-out version of the automated-research loop Patrick raises, against Altman’s expectation that researchers stay relevant through it.

item.title: The Easy Interval Method: Intervals Every Day, Run Easy
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In this 13-minute explainer, Terry O’Hare, a masters runner from Ireland who runs the Faster Master channel, lays out the Easy Interval Method (EIM), a training system devised by Dutch coach Herman Verheul in the 1970s and developed by Dutch 5,000 m runner Klaas Lok [1]. The pitch is counterintuitive: instead of building a base from long, slow endurance runs, you run intervals almost every day, but at a sub-threshold pace, with recoveries long enough that you can back it up the next day.

The main points, each linking to the supporting part of the transcript:

  • The workload is survivable because of pace and recovery. Intervals run six days a week are possible because they sit at sub-threshold pace with a recovery jog roughly equal to the rep, plus a short walk at each end, so you can complete the session today and repeat it tomorrow.
  • The long recovery is the point. Far from being a concession, an 800–1,000 m jog recovery covers real aerobic mileage a static 90-second rest never would, which is why critics who want to shorten it miss what the system is doing.
  • Even skeptics can steal the surges. If daily intervals aren’t for you, adding short pickups (surges) to an ordinary long run captures much of the benefit and turns the run into an impromptu fartlek.

My Notes

  • Where the easy mileage goes. EIM accumulates aerobic stimulus without the neuromuscular cost of hard intervals or the staleness of slow steady running. The recovery jog does the easy-volume work that steady-state runs do in a conventional plan, while the daily reps keep some pace and leg reactivity in the system. That is why “intervals every day” is less reckless than it first sounds, once you see where the easy mileage goes.
  • Versus Norwegian singles. The contrast Terry draws with the Norwegian singles method is the useful reference point for anyone who has met that trend. Both hold reps at sub-threshold, and the only real difference is scheduling. Norwegian singles pack the sub-threshold work into a few days and fill the rest with easy running. EIM spreads it across almost every day and lets the long recovery jog absorb the easy running.
  • The evidence caveat. What the video lacks is evidence. The case rests on one athlete’s palmares, one masters record-holder, and a coach’s rationale, with no controlled comparison against a matched training plan. That is normal for training-methodology content, but a reader deciding whether to switch should treat the mechanism story as plausible rather than proven, and ramp in gradually as Terry himself insists.

Transcript

What’s here is the video’s auto-generated transcript, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The spoken words are preserved; three layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

  • Topic outline. The video has no official YouTube chapters, so the [12] section headings below are my own segmentation of the talk. Each links to the video at the timestamp where that section begins.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of a salient name, concept, or product links to an authoritative source.
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag a claim worth confirming or a spot where the auto-captions garbled a figure.

This is a single-speaker video, so there are no per-paragraph speaker labels — the whole body is Terry O’Hare talking. Because the source is auto-captions, punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks are editorial (ASR ships without them), and obvious mishearings of names and terms are corrected silently — e.g. the captions’ Class Lactate, EAM, and EIAM are rendered as Klaas Lok, EIM, and the garbled PSS 4 200 m as paces for 200 m.

0:00 — The club-runner rut, and a Dutch alternative

A lot of runners, particularly club runners, training 5 or 6 days a week, can get into a bit of a cycle of long run Sunday, during the week maybe one, two speed sessions Tuesday and Thursday, and the rest of the week they just fill in with long, easy, or recovery runs. And of course, time has shown that this can work for many of us. But is there a better way?

Well, back in the 1970s, Dutch coach Herman Verheul, I think that’s how you pronounce it, turned traditional thinking on its head. Instead of slow, easy endurance runs as the basis of all training, he introduced a system consisting almost entirely of interval training. It was then popularized and continually developed by Dutch 5,000 m runner Klaas Lok, and it is now widely known as EIM, easy interval method. So, if your training has become a bit monotonous, or your race times have stagnated, perhaps it’s time to look at a different approach.

I’m Terry O’Hare, a masters runner from Ireland. This is the Faster Masters channel, and if you haven’t already done so, it would really help the channel if you give it a thumbs up like, and hit the subscribe button. Thank you.

1:24 — What the method actually is

So, let’s look at this in a bit more depth. It could be said, and has been said, that lots of long, slow endurance runs create long, slow endurance runners. But are intervals 6 days a week a real, viable alternative? Is it actually possible?

In the EIM, sustained easy or steady-state runs are virtually nonexistent. For all distances other than the marathon, and occasionally the half marathon, the traditional weekly long run disappears too. And even when included, in the marathon schedules, it will contain surges. More of that later.

2:05 — Why daily intervals are possible: easy pace and long recovery

So is it physically possible to run intervals every day, six days a week, without breaking down very quickly? Well, the clue is in the name, easy, and made possible by both the pace of the run and the length of the recovery period.

The intervals, normally 200 m, 400 m, and 1,000 m repeats, with the occasional 2,000, will have an equal or near-equal recovery. So 200s will have a 200 easy recovery, 400s will have a 400 recovery, and 1,000 m repeats will have 800, maybe even 1,000 m recovery. And furthermore, at the finish of each rep, you will actually walk 30 to 40 m, and walk again before the start of the next one.

Then there’s the speed of each interval. These are not run at the pace we would normally consider interval pace. Instead, these are very much sub-threshold pace — a bit of a buzzword at the moment with the Norwegian singles — but I’ll give you some idea of the actual pace times in a minute so you get the idea.

3:08 — A sample half-marathon week

Let’s look at a typical week’s training for a runner preparing for a half marathon and training six days a week. Sunday, and being a half marathon program, there is actually a moderate endurance run here, 14 to 18K, but with surges, which we’re going to look at later, and also three to five times 100 m strides. Monday, 10 by 400. Tuesday, six by 1,000. Wednesday, six by 1,000. Thursday, 15 by 200s. Friday, six by 1,000. And a rest day Saturday. And there’s a few strides thrown in there three or four days a week, whenever you can manage it. And the intervals Monday to Friday would of course have three or 4 k warm-up and the same cool-down.

Now, before you say that’s excessive, just remember these intervals are not run at your 3k or 5k race pace with a 60s and 90-second recovery. No, they’re run very much at a sub-threshold pace.

4:11 — How it differs from Norwegian singles

So, are these similar to Norwegian singles? Well, Norwegian singles are also run at a sub-threshold pace, maybe a little quicker, but the big difference is in the recovery. The recovery with the EIM is designed so that you can recover sufficiently, not only to finish the session, but to do it again tomorrow and the next day and the next day, five or six times a week. With Norwegian singles, you do them all on three separate days a week and just fill in the rest with easy recovery runs.

4:42 — Pace comparison: Daniels’ VDOT versus Lok’s charts

Maybe the easiest way to demonstrate the actual pace would be to compare interval times calculated, for example, by renowned coach Jack Daniels and his VDOT system with Klaas Lok’s EIM times. Let’s take a 40-minute 10k runner as an example. Using the well-known Jack Daniels VDOT charts, 1,000 intervals for a 40-minute 10k runner would be run at between 3:43 and 3:55 pace. With Klaas Lok’s EIM system, these would be run at 4:14 to 4:31 pace. A substantial difference.

And furthermore, Daniels would recommend a recovery time equal to about half of the time of the interval. So, in this example, about 2 minutes. Whereas with the easy interval method, you would have an 800-meter recovery plus a little walk at the start and finish, maybe looking at 6, 7 minutes. All of a sudden, it looks a bit — or a lot — easier. And there would be a similar percentage difference in the paces for 200 m and 400 m intervals.

5:45 — Easing in, and the claimed benefits

Nevertheless, even though this is beginning to sound a lot easier than at first sight, there is no way that someone doing four, five easy runs a week could switch to this immediately. You would definitely have to introduce it gradually. If you’re already doing, however, one or two faster workouts a week, consider changing those to 1,000 m repeats, and you would actually find that easier. Then you’d be in a position to consider adding a third day for a few weeks, maybe 400s.

So, the claimed advantages to using this system would be more reactivity in the legs from running at a faster than easy pace. That in turn would give a better running economy and improved biomechanics. The ability to run at a higher speed without excess lactate in the muscles. And you’d be fitter and better prepared for races. Is it suited for masters runners? I think it’s ideal for masters runners to maintain your speed and reactive running.

6:48 — Why the recoveries are so long

Why are the recovery periods so long? Critics will say that 800 m or 1,000 m jog recovery is far too long, and the intervals at that sub-threshold pace could be done with 60 to 90-second recovery. But this longer recovery is as crucial to the system as the pace. A full 800, 1,000 m jog provides far greater aerobic stimulus than a static 90-second rest, simply due to the actual mileage being covered.

And remember that, just as with normal intervals, where you don’t do the first few too hard and then struggle to complete the session, they need to be at this easy controlled pace not only to complete the session today, but to repeat it tomorrow and the next day and the next day. This is high-end aerobic training at its best, and this is the key.

7:51 — Surges: the one long run, done differently

I mentioned earlier that one long endurance run is included in the marathon training and sometimes in the half marathon schedule. But there’s a slight, or big, important difference to how this is run. Every endurance run includes surges. Now, surges are when you pick up the pace to maybe 10k race pace for 30 to 60 seconds every 5 to 7 minutes.

I’ve tried this. What I do is when my Garmin beeps at each kilometer, I pick up the pace for 200 m, back off again. Simple as that. And what a difference that makes to your run. Doing this on a long run over varied terrain almost turns this into a fartlek session, in that I have no idea before I start where the 1k markers are going to hit. They could be on a nice flat even surface, or they could be at the bottom of a steep hill. And that makes the run more fun.

I regularly do a 20k run like this. I use the first 2k of that as a warm-up and then add the 200 surges each kilometer, and I end up with a 20k run that has included 18 by 200s at about 10k pace without noticing any extra effort. It’s a very useful workout that is fun and it’s over before you realize it.

You can look at this system and decide all those intervals are not for me. At least take the surges out of this. Add them into your long run. They will transform your long run and you will enjoy it.

9:25 — No VO2 max work, and racing as the anaerobic stimulus

As I mentioned earlier, this is high-end aerobic training. There is no VO2 max workout here, and that could be an issue for some. Klaas himself raced very regularly and used a lot of those races as anaerobic workouts. And regular racing is almost assumed with this system. For those who don’t, including myself, there are anaerobic sessions included in the plans, and to be used particularly in the build-up to racing.

9:57 — Who it suits: Lok, masters reactivity, and Dan King

So, who is this type of training suited to? Well, Klaas Lok himself admits, or claims, that he was not naturally very talented or gifted, but he still used to win 26 Dutch national titles, including six cross-country championships, a 10,000 m title, a 1,500 m title, and a European indoor silver in the 3,000 m in 1980.

Note

Editor’s note. The auto-captions garble the specific personal-best times Terry lists here (the raw ASR reads “a 20 at 24 10,000 m, a 330 at 1,500 m”), so the mistranscribed numbers have been dropped rather than guessed at. See the book for Lok’s actual bests.

Now, some coaches believe that us masters runners shouldn’t be doing interval training at all because our muscle reactivity has declined with age, but EIM actually promotes the opposite. Reactivity is a basic essential which should be maintained at your highest possible personal level. Not only are strong reactive muscles faster, they’re also less prone to injury.

A masters runner you might have heard of who is an exponent of the EIM is Dan King, a US male 60 to 65 runner who, in one day in 2020, set a world mile record of 4:52, an American record of 9:58 in the 3,000 m, and a US 5,000 m record of 16:48. And yes, all in one day.

Note

Editor’s note. This checks out: on December 11, 2020, Dan King (then 61) ran 4:52 for the mile, 9:58.47 for the 3,000 m, and 16:48.67 for the 5,000 m in a single day, the latter two ratified as M60 American records (per Runner’s World and Bring Back the Mile). Age-group records move, so treat “world record” as of that date.

11:31 — The book and the community

To get a complete insight into this system, you really need to read this book, unsurprisingly titled The Easy Interval Method [1]. It really is a bible, and it’s a mine of information. I just flicked through a few pages and you’ll see how well worn it is with me. I refer to it almost on a daily basis. It contains everything: schedules from 800 m to marathon. It has pace charts, everything you would ever need as a runner. Have a look on Google for this, The Easy Interval Method by Klaas Lok. And it has schedules for runners who can only commit to 3 days a week right up to those who want to train 7, 8 times a week. Buy it, you will not regret it.

Buying the book will give you access to the Facebook group where ex-runners of the system and Klaas Lok himself will answer your questions, respond to your comments, which is incredibly useful as you progress through a training plan.

So, if you enjoyed this video, please hit the subscribe button, you know it makes sense. And if you want to find out more about the alternative Norwegian singles training, watch my most successful ever video here. And of course, don’t forget to look at our brand new website, thefastermaster.com. For now, though, thank you for watching.

References

Talk and source

  • Build massive aerobic fitness with the best training system you’ve never heard of! — the Faster Master, June 30, 2026 (13 min).

People

  • Terry O’Hare / the Faster Master — masters runner from Ireland; the video’s presenter.
  • Klaas Lok — Dutch 5,000 m runner and coach who developed and popularized the Easy Interval Method.
  • Herman Verheul — Dutch coach who originated the interval-based approach in the 1970s that became the EIM.
  • Jack Daniels — running coach and physiologist; creator of the VDOT system referenced in the pace comparison.
  • Dan King — US M60 runner cited as an EIM exponent.

Concepts and background

  • Interval training
  • Lactate threshold (the “sub-threshold” pace target)
  • VO2 max
  • Running economy
  • Fartlek
  • Norwegian singles method — the contemporary sub-threshold approach Terry contrasts with EIM.

Book

  1. Lok, Klaas. The Easy Interval Method. Meyer & Meyer Sport, 2019. Official site: https://easyintervalmethod.com/

item.title: Karen Hao on Empire of AI: OpenAI, AGI Believers, and a New Colonialism
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In a June 2025 episode of Novara Media’s Downstream, Aaron Bastani interviews Karen Hao — the MIT Technology Review and Wall Street Journal reporter who covered OpenAI for years — about her book Empire of AI, built on more than 300 interviews, over 150 of them with current and former OpenAI staff. The conversation runs about 90 minutes and is less a tour of the technology than a structural argument: that a handful of AI labs are behaving like the old corporate empires, and that letting a small group concentrate this much power over data, energy, water, and labor is, in Hao’s word, “structurally unsound.”

A few takeaways, each linking to the supporting chapter below:

  • “AI” is a suitcase word that hides enormous differences in scale and cost. Hao’s analogy is “transportation,” which can mean a bicycle or a rocket, and politicians who promise “more AI” rarely say which one they mean.
  • The environmental bill is paid locally: data centers cool themselves with public drinking water and run largely on fossil power, so the cost lands on particular communities — a record drought in Montevideo, a housing-construction ban along the UK’s M4 corridor.
  • The race runs on ideology as much as economics: with no clear business case, what sustains the spending is a genuine, quasi-religious belief that recreating human intelligence is the most important thing anyone could do.
  • OpenAI began as an open nonprofit and inverted every founding commitment once it decided that scale, not talent, was the bottleneck. Converting to capture capital is what split Musk and Altman.
  • Nobody could tell Hao what Sam Altman believes: across 150 OpenAI interviews, the recurring account is that Altman reflects whatever the person in front of him believes — at once his fundraising gift and the root of his polarizing reputation.
  • The supply chain looks colonial: Kenyan content moderators and Venezuelan data labelers paid a few dollars an hour at one end, million-dollar pay packages and multi-trillion-dollar valuations at the other.
  • Colossal scale is a choice the labs made: DeepSeek and Stable Diffusion reached frontier-level results with far less compute, undercutting the premise that giant data centers are required to build capable AI.
  • The response is to contest the supply chain: data, land, water, and the schools and offices where AI gets deployed are all publicly contestable, and Hao’s optimism rests on people pushing back at every node.

With the help of AI, I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — the YouTube auto-captions, content-diarized into speaker turns and sliced into the interview’s chapters and finer topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for what’s verbatim and what’s editorial.

YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

  • 0:00:00 — Intro (YouTube)
  • 0:03:11 — AI, deep learning, and machine learning explained (YouTube)
  • 0:09:27 — Data centres and resource consumption (YouTube)
  • 0:14:30 — Who are the major players (YouTube)
  • 0:23:17 — What’s behind OpenAI’s rapid rise (YouTube)
  • 0:32:50 — Who is Sam Altman? (YouTube)
  • 0:45:40 — Who is Karen Hao? (YouTube)
  • 0:51:49 — Colonial similarities to AI companies (YouTube)
  • 1:07:39 — DeepSeek (YouTube)
  • 1:11:49 — Exploitative practices in the Global South (YouTube)
  • 1:22:00 — How to stop Big Tech (YouTube)

Transcript

What’s here is the YouTube auto-caption transcript, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog itself is verbatim — no words added, cut, or reworded — but several layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

  • Speaker attribution and chapter + topic outline. This interview’s auto-captions ship with no speaker markers, so the split into Aaron Bastani (host) and Karen Hao (guest) turns was reconstructed by reading the dialog; a stray line may be mislabeled. The 11 YouTube chapters each link to their timestamp and are sliced into finer topic subsections whose titles are editorial summaries, not verbatim quotes. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
  • Punctuation is editorial. Auto-captions arrive without reliable punctuation, capitalization, or paragraph breaks; those are added here. Obvious mishearings of proper nouns and technical terms are corrected silently — e.g. Karen How → Karen Hao, Sam Alman/Melman → Sam Altman, Ilas Sutskever/Sudskver → Ilya Sutskever, chat GBT → ChatGPT, Enthropic → Anthropic, Peter Teal → Peter Thiel, Satia Nadella → Satya Nadella, BYU → Baidu, Marate Shake → Marietje Schaake, Angus Hansen → Angus Hanton, Jonathan hate → Jonathan Haidt, dolly → DALL·E, Larry and Jihad → Butlerian Jihad.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of every salient person, company, product, paper, or concept links to an authoritative source.
  • Bracketed acronym expansions. Where an acronym appears first without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] to mark the addition as editorial.
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag figures and secondhand claims a reader might want to sanity-check, and add background where the dialog asserts something without explaining it.
  • Numbered references. The one formal paper cited has a [[N]](#ref-N) cite linking to the References block at the bottom.

0:00:00 — Intro

The episode opens cold on a clip pulled from later in the interview, then Aaron Bastani’s scripted voiceover introduction, before the conversation proper begins.

Karen Hao: I went to school with a lot of the people that now build these technologies. I went to school with some of the executives at OpenAI. I don’t find these figures to be towering or magical. Like, I remember when we were walking around dorm rooms together in our pajamas, and it instilled in me this understanding that technology is always a product of human choices.

And different humans will have different blind spots. And if you give a small group of those people too much power to develop technologies that will affect billions of people’s lives, inevitably that is structurally unsound.

Aaron Bastani: Artificial intelligence is the backbone of some of the biggest companies in the world right now. Multi-trillion-dollar companies can talk about nothing else but AI. And of course, whenever it’s discussed in the media, by politicians and civil society, it’s compared invariably to the steam engine. It is going to be the backbone for a new machine age.

Some people are really optimistic about the possibilities it will bring. They are the boosters, the techno-optimists, the techno-utopians. Others are doomers. They’re down on AI. AGI [artificial general intelligence], it’s never going to happen. And if it does, well, it’s going to look like The Matrix, or maybe even The Terminator and Skynet. We don’t want that, do we?

Today’s guest, however, is not speculating about the future. Instead, they’re very much immersed in the present, and indeed the recent past, of the artificial intelligence industry.

Karen Hao went to MIT. She studied mechanical engineering. She knows the STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] game inside out. But she made a choice to go into journalism and media, to talk about these issues with a fluency and a knowledge that very few people have.

Rather than speculate, what Karen has done with this book is talk to people in the field. 300 interviews with 260 people in the industry, 150 interviews with 90 employees of OpenAI, both past and present. She has access to emails, company Slack channels, the works.

This is the inside account of OpenAI and the perils of artificial intelligence, big tech, and big money coming after, well, pretty much everything. It’s an amazing story told incredibly well. I hope you enjoy this interview.

Karen Hao, welcome to Downstream.

Karen Hao: Thank you so much for having me, Aaron.

Aaron Bastani: It’s a real pleasure to have you on. Right — we say that to everybody, every guest. But I have to say, and this has had rave reviews, even though I’ve lost the dust jacket — Empire of AI, with this huge poem you’ve written, 421 pages, I think, not including the acknowledgements. Really, really interesting book. It’s about AI, this burgeoning industry in the United States around artificial intelligence. That word has been in circulation since the 1950s, I believe.

0:03:11 — AI, deep learning, and machine learning explained

Why “AI” resists definition: a marketing term from 1956

Aaron Bastani: Yeah. Before we drill down into your book — what is AI, and what do people mean by AI when they talk about it in 2025 in Silicon Valley?

Karen Hao: This is — you would think this is the easiest question, but this is always the hardest question that I get, because artificial intelligence is quite poorly defined.

We’ll go back first to 1956, because I feel like it helps understand a little bit about why it’s so poorly defined today. The term was originally coined in 1956 by this Dartmouth professor, assistant professor John McCarthy. And he coined it to draw more attention and more money to research that he was originally doing under a different name.

And that was something he has explicitly said a few decades later. He said, “I invented the term artificial intelligence to get money for a summer study.” And that marketing route to the phrase is part of why it’s really difficult to pin down a specific definition today.

The other reason is because generally people say that AI refers to the concept of recreating human intelligence in computers. But we also don’t have a scientific consensus around what human intelligence is. So quite literally, when people say AI, they’re referring to an umbrella of all these different types of technologies that appear to simulate different human behaviors or human tasks.

But it really ranges from something like Siri on your iPhone all the way to ChatGPT, which behind the scenes are actually really, really different ways of operating. They’re totally different scales in terms of the consumption of the technologies. And of course they often have different use cases as well.

Note

Editor’s note. McCarthy’s “get money for a summer study” line refers to the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, the workshop proposal — co-authored with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon — that coined the term. McCarthy was an assistant professor at Dartmouth at the time.

Aaron Bastani: So right now, when OpenAI, Meta, when they use those words “AI” in regards to their products specifically — what are they talking about?

Karen Hao: Most often they are now talking about what are called deep learning systems. So these are systems that train on loads of data, and you have software that can statistically compute the patterns in that data, and then that model is used to make decisions, or generate text, or make predictions. So most modern-day AI systems built by companies like Meta, by OpenAI, by Google are now these deep learning systems.

Aaron Bastani: So deep learning is the same as machine learning is the same as neural networks? These are synonyms?

Karen Hao: Deep learning is a subcategory of machine learning. Machine learning refers to a specific branch of AI where you build software that calculates patterns in data. Deep learning is when you’re specifically using neural networks to calculate those patterns.

So — one of the founding fathers of AI used to call AI a “suitcase word.” Because you can put whatever you want in the suitcase, and suddenly AI means something different.

So we have this suitcase word of AI, and then under that, any data-driven AI techniques are called machine learning, and then any neural-network data-driven techniques are called deep learning. So it’s the smallest circle within this broader suitcase word.

Aaron Bastani: So deep learning and neural networks are kind of interchangeable.

Karen Hao: Not exactly, in the sense that neural networks are referring to a piece of software, and deep learning is referring to the process that the software is doing, right?

The “transportation” analogy: politicians who promise “more AI”

Aaron Bastani: Yeah. Do you get upset when politicians — so in this country we have a prime minister called Keir, you know — and they say, “We think the NHS can save, you know, 20% by using AI applications”? Do you sort of think, “My goodness, these people have no idea what they’re talking about,” because that is such an expansive term? Its political convenience is precisely that it doesn’t mean anything.

Karen Hao: It does frustrate me a little bit. I often use the analogy that AI is like the word “transportation.” I mean, transportation can refer to bicycles, or rockets, or self-driving cars, or gas-guzzling trucks — they’re all different modes of transportation, serve different purposes, different cost-benefit analyses.

And you would never have a politician say, “We need more transportation to mitigate climate change.” You would be like, “But what kind of — what are you talking about?” Or, “We need more transportation to stimulate the economy.”

There is a vagueness around the AI discussion that is really unproductive, and I think a lot of that leads to confusion where people think AI equals one thing, and AI equals progress, and so we should just have all of it.

But actually, if we were to use the transportation analogy — you know, having more bicycles, having more public transit, sounds great. But if someone were actually referring to just using rockets to commute from Dublin to London, and we were like, “Everyone should get a rocket now, that’s going to bring us more progress,” you’d be like, “What are you talking about?” And that’s effectively what these companies are doing with general intelligence.

Aaron Bastani: When you’re giving people tools for free with regards to generative AI to just generate stupid images of nonsense — that’s kind of what we’re doing, right? I presume you would take that analogy to that level. It’s like saying, “Let’s use a rocket to get from Dublin to London to Paris.”

Karen Hao: Yeah, exactly. It’s not fit for the task. And the extraordinary amount of environmental costs for flying that rocket, when you could have flown a much more efficient plane to do the same thing, is like — what are you doing?

And that’s one of the things that people don’t really realize about generative AI: the resource consumption required to develop these models, and also to use these models, is quite extraordinary. And oftentimes people are using them for tasks that could be achieved with highly efficient different AI techniques.

But because we use the sweeping term “AI” to mean anything, people just think, “Oh yeah, right, I’m just going to use ChatGPT for my one-stop-shop solution for anything AI-related.”

0:09:27 — Data centres and resource consumption

Projected energy demand: McKinsey’s “half to 1.2 times the UK’s annual consumption”

Aaron Bastani: So right now, data centers globally, I think, are about 3–3.5% of CO₂ emissions. The data centers for AI are a tiny fraction of that, but obviously they’re growing at an extraordinary pace. Are there any numbers out there with regards to projected CO₂ emissions of data centers globally 5, 10, 15 years from now? Or is it so recent that we can’t really speculate about the numbers involved?

Note

Editor’s note. Estimates vary by what’s being counted. Data centers are usually put at roughly 1–1.5% of global electricity use (the IEA’s figure for 2022 was about 1–1.3%, excluding crypto mining); the higher “2–4%” figures generally refer to the broader information-and-communications-technology sector, not data centers alone. Aaron’s “3–3.5% of CO₂ emissions” is at the upper end of what’s typically cited.

Karen Hao: There are numbers around the energy consumption, which you could then use to try and project carbon emissions. There was a McKinsey report that recently projected that, based on the current pace of data center and supercomputer expansion for the development and deployment of AI technologies, we would need to add around half to 1.2 times the amount of energy consumed in the UK annually to the global grid in the next 5 years.

Aaron Bastani: Wow.

Karen Hao: And most of that will be serviced by fossil fuels. This is something that Sam Altman actually even said in front of the Senate a couple of weeks ago. He said it will most probably be natural gas — so he picked the nicest fossil fuel.

But we’re already seeing reports of coal plants having their lives extended. They were meant to be retired, but they’re no longer being retired, explicitly to power data center development.

We’re seeing reports of Elon Musk’s xAI — the giant supercomputer that he built called Colossus, in Memphis, Tennessee — it is being powered with around 35 unlicensed methane gas turbines that are pumping thousands of toxic air pollutants into that community.

So this data center acceleration is not just accelerating the climate crisis; it’s also accelerating the public health crisis of people’s ability to access clean air as well as clean water.

Note

Editor’s note. The Colossus turbine count traces to reporting by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which used aerial imagery to count roughly 35 gas turbines at the Memphis site, many without the Clean Air Act permits the SELC argued were required. xAI has said it brought turbines on site to meet near-term power needs while grid capacity was built out.

Fresh water for cooling, and the Montevideo drought

Karen Hao: One of the aspects that’s really under-talked-about with this kind of AI development — the OpenAI version of AI development — is that these data centers need fresh water to cool, because if they used any other kind of water it would corrode the equipment, it would lead to bacterial growth. And so most often these data centers actually use public drinking water, because when they enter into a community, that is the infrastructure that’s already laid to deliver fresh water to companies, to businesses, to residents.

One of the things that I highlight in my book is there are many communities that do not have sufficient drinking water even for people. I went to Montevideo, Uruguay, to speak with people about a historic level of drought they were experiencing, where the Montevideo government literally did not have enough water to put into the public drinking water supply. So they were mixing toxic waste water in, just so people could have something come out of their taps when they opened them.

And for people that were too poor to buy bottled water, that is what they were drinking. And women were having higher rates of miscarriages, elderly were having an exacerbation of their chronic diseases. And in the middle of that, Google proposed to build a data center that would use more drinking water.

Aaron Bastani: This is potable water, right? You can’t use seawater, because of the saline aspect.

Karen Hao: Exactly. And Bloomberg recently had a story that said two-thirds of the data centers now being built for AI development are in fact going into water[-stressed areas].

Note

Editor’s note. The figure is from a December 2024 Bloomberg investigation, which found that roughly two-thirds of new data centers built or in development since 2022 are in places with high water stress.

“Unlicensed,” and the erosion-of-democracy thesis

Aaron Bastani: You said a moment ago about xAI’s unlicensed energy generation using methane gas. When you say “unlicensed,” what do you mean?

Karen Hao: As in the company just decided to completely ignore existing environmental regulations when they installed those methane gas turbines. And this is actually one of the things that I concluded by the end of my reporting: not only are these companies really corporate empires, but also that if we allow them to be unfettered in their access to resources and unfettered in their expansion, they will ultimately erode democracy. That is the greatest threat of their behaviors.

And what xAI is doing is a perfect example, at the smallest level — these companies are entering into communities and completely hijacking existing laws, existing regulations, existing democratic processes to build the infrastructure for their expansion. And we’re seeing this hijacking of the democratic process at every level, from the smallest local levels all the way to the international level.

Aaron Bastani: It’s that orthodoxy of “seek permission after you do something” — when you start applying this, this is business as usual for those companies. That’s part of their expansion strategy, which we’ll talk about — and we’re going to talk about the sort of global colonial aspect as well with regards to resource consumption, resource use.

0:14:30 — Who are the major players

The players: US labs, the Chinese ecosystem, and Europe’s “tiddlers”

Aaron Bastani: Just to bring it back to the US again, because at the top of this conversation I want to offer a bit of a primer to people out there who maybe know what AI is, maybe have used ChatGPT — what are the major companies we’re now talking about in this space, particularly in the United States, over the last 5 years?

Who are the people in this race to AGI — allegedly artificial general intelligence, something which either might be sentient (probably not) or capable of augmenting its own intelligence (more plausible)? Who are the major players in that field right now?

Karen Hao: One caveat on AGI is that it’s as ill-defined as the term AI, so I like to think of it as just a rebranding. The entire history of AI has just been about rebranding, and the term “deep learning” was also a rebranding. So, anyway.

But the players: first, OpenAI, of course — they were the ones that fired the first shot with ChatGPT. Anthropic, major competitor. Google, Meta, Microsoft — they’re the older internet giants that are now also racing to deploy these technologies. Safe Superintelligence, which spun out of OpenAI — there are many OpenAI splinters — this was founded very recently by the former chief scientist of OpenAI [Ilya Sutskever]. And Thinking Machines Lab, founded very recently by a former chief technology officer of OpenAI.

And Amazon is now trying to get into the game as well, and Apple is also trying to get in the game. So basically all the older-generation tech giants, as well as a new crop of AI players, are all jostling in this space.

Aaron Bastani: And that’s just the US, right?

Karen Hao: And that’s just the US. The Chinese ecosystem is interesting, because they don’t really use the term AGI. This is a very unique thing about the US ecosystem — that there’s a quasi-religious fervor that underpins the construction of AI products and services, whereas in China it’s much more like, these are businesses, we’re building products that users are going to use.

So if you’re just looking at companies building chatbots that are sort of akin to ChatGPT, then we’re talking about ByteDance, owner of TikTok; Alibaba, the equivalent of Amazon; Baidu, the equivalent of Google; Huawei, the equivalent of Apple; and Tencent — what is the equivalent of Tencent? I guess Meta is the equivalent of Tencent. So they’re also building these things. And there’s similarly a crop of startups moving into the generative AI space.

Aaron Bastani: And in Europe, we’ve got the little tiddlers, like Mistral in France — really not at the races, ’cause we’re Europe.

What’s the business case for all this? Because obviously you’ve got massive companies often driven by maximizing shareholder value, multi-trillion-dollar valuations. You do these things, you invest money to make money, as a capitalist society.

So what is the business case made by, say, Microsoft when they have their shareholder meetings and they say, “We’re going to allocate $40, $50 billion towards building data centers”?

No clear business case — so what sustains it is ideology

Karen Hao: It’s interesting that you mentioned Microsoft, because Microsoft has recently been pulling back their investments in data centers. They went all in, and now they’re rapidly starting to abandon data center projects.

So to answer your question, it is really unclear what the business case is, and Microsoft has been one of the first companies to start acknowledging that. The East India Company analogy

Karen Hao: That is the analogy that I have increasingly started using, especially with the Trump administration in power, because the British East India Company very much was a corporate empire, and started off not very imperial. They just started off as a company, a very small company based in London. And of course, through economic trade agreements with India, gained significant economic power, political power, and eventually became the apex predator in that ecosystem — and that’s when they started being very imperial in nature.

And they were, the entire time, abetted by the British Empire, the nation-state empire. So you have a corporate empire, you have a nation-state empire, and I literally see that dynamic playing out now, where the US government is also in its empire era. The Trump administration has quite literally used words to suggest that he wants to expand and fortify the American empire, and he sees these corporate empires like OpenAI as his empire-building assets.

And so I think he is probably seeing it in the same way that the British crown saw the British East India Company: let’s just let this company acquire all these resources, do all these things, and then eventually we’ll nationalize the company — and then India formally becomes a colony of the British Empire.

So whatever the modern-day equivalent would be of nationalizing these companies is Trump’s endgame. He is helping them strike all these deals and installing all this American hardware and software all around the world, with the hope that then those become national assets.

So I don’t ultimately know who’s going to win — the nation-state empire or the corporate empire. But either version is bad, because all of the people in power now, both the business executives and the politicians, do not actually care at all about preserving democracy.

What DeepSeek showed: frontier capability at a fraction of the compute

And some people argue that ultimately they were distilling the models that were first developed through the scaling paradigm. So you first develop some of these colossal scaling models, and then you end up making them smaller and more efficient. So some people argue that you actually have to first do that scaling before you get the efficiency.

Note

Editor’s note. DeepSeek reported that the final training run for its V3 model (671 billion total parameters, 37 billion active per token) cost about $5.6 million in compute — orders of magnitude below the figures associated with comparable US models. That number is the headline final-run cost only; it excludes prior research, failed runs, and the cost of the GPU cluster itself, which is why “$5.6M built DeepSeek” is often called misleading.

Why US labs won’t economize: monopoly logic and path dependence

Aaron Bastani: Why? Do they like giving their money to Nvidia?

Karen Hao: Because when you continue to pursue a scaling approach, and you’re the only one with all of the AI experts in the world, you persuade people into believing this is the only path, and therefore you continue to monopolize this technology, because it locks out anyone else from playing that game.

And also because of path dependence — these companies are actually not that nimble. It’s not so easy for them to just immediately swap to a different approach.

They end up putting in motion all the resources, all of the training runs, so on and so forth, over the course of months, and then they just have to run with it.

The Stable Diffusion precedent — and Jensen Huang’s charisma

Karen Hao: So DeepSeek actually wasn’t the first time this happened. The first time was with image generators and Stable Diffusion. And Stable Diffusion was specifically developed by an academic in Europe who was really pissed that the AI companies like OpenAI were taking a scaling approach to image generation.

He was like, this is literally wholly unnecessary. And they’re spending thousands of chips, all of this energy, to produce DALL·E. And ultimately, he ended up producing Stable Diffusion with a couple hundred chips, using a new technique called latent diffusion [1], hence the name Stable Diffusion.

And arguably it was actually an even better model than DALL·E, because users were saying that Stable Diffusion had even better image quality, better image generation, better ability to actually control the images than DALL·E.

But even knowing that latent diffusion existed, OpenAI continued to develop DALL·E with these massive scaling approaches. And it wasn’t until later that they adopted the cheaper version. But it was significantly delayed. And I was asking OpenAI researchers, like, why? That doesn’t make any sense, why did you do that? And they were like, well, once you set off on a path, it’s kind of hard to pivot.

Also, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, is really charismatic, right? It’s quite funny, because — I’m a Marxist, I’m going to make that confession — you have these big structural understandings of how history happens, and then you sort of realize, actually, this guy’s really charismatic, and this person’s really manipulative, and all of a sudden the world’s hyperpower is making these technological decisions. Kenya: building OpenAI’s content-moderation filter

Aaron Bastani: We talked about data centers, we talked about earth, water, energy. I want to talk also about some of the more exploitative practices with regards to workers in the Global South. Karen Hao: Yeah. So I ended up interviewing workers in Kenya who were contracted by OpenAI to build a content moderation filter for the company. And at that point in the company’s history, it was starting to think about commercialization, after coming from its nonprofit fundamental-AI-research roots. And they realized, if we’re going to put a text generation model in the hands of millions of users, it’s going to be a PR crisis if it starts spewing racist, toxic, hateful speech.

In fact, in 2016, Microsoft infamously did exactly this. They developed a chatbot named Tay. They put it online without any content moderation, and then within hours it started saying awful things, and they had to take it offline. And to this day — as evidenced by me bringing it up — it’s still brought up as a horrible case study in corporate mismanagement.

And so OpenAI thought, we don’t want to do that, we’re going to create a filter that wraps around our models, so that even if the models start generating this stuff, it never reaches the user, because the filter blocks it.

In order to build that filter, what the Kenyan workers had to do was wade through reams of the worst text on the internet, as well as AI-generated text where OpenAI was prompting its models to imagine the worst text on the internet. And the workers then had to go through all of this and put it into a detailed taxonomy: is this hate speech, is this harassment, is this violent content, is this sexual content? And the degree of hate speech, of violence, of sexual content. So they were asking workers to say, does it involve sexual abuse? Does it involve sexual abuse of children? So on and so forth.

And to this day, I believe if you look at OpenAI’s content moderation filter documentation, it actually lists all of those categories. And this is one of the things that it offers to business clients of their models — that you can toggle on and off each of these filters. So that’s why they had to put this into that taxonomy.

Mophat: when the trauma breaks a family

Karen Hao: The workers ended up suffering very many of the same symptoms as content moderators of the social media era. Absolutely traumatized by the work, completely changed their personalities, left them with PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]. And I highlight the story of this man Mophat, one of the workers I interviewed, who showed to me that it’s not just individuals that break down — it’s their families and communities, because there are people who rely on these individuals.

Mophat was on the sexual content team. His personality totally changed as he was reading child sexual abuse every day. And when he came home, he stopped playing with his stepdaughter, he stopped being intimate with his wife.

And he also couldn’t explain to them why he was changing, because he didn’t know how to say to them, “I read sex content all day.” That doesn’t sound like a real job — it sounds like a very shameful job. ChatGPT hadn’t come out yet, so there was no conception of what that even meant.

And so one day, his wife asks him for fish for dinner. He goes out, buys three fish — one for him, one for her, one for the stepdaughter — and by the time he comes home, all of their bags are packed and they’re completely gone. And she texts him, “I don’t know the man you’ve become anymore, and I’m never coming back.”

Venezuela: the “crisis playbook” and the queue

Aaron Bastani: And then on the other side of the Atlantic, you talk about people in South America doing effectively, you know, Mechanical Turk piece-work for these companies as well. Can you talk about that a little bit?

Karen Hao: Yeah. So generative AI is not the only thing that leads to data annotation. This has actually been part of the AI industry for a very long time. And so I ended up, years ago, interviewing this woman in Colombia who was a Venezuelan refugee, about the specific thing that happened to her country in the global AI supply chain.

So in 2016, when the AI industry first started actually looking into the development of self-driving cars, there was a surge in demand for highly educated workers to do data annotation labeling for helping self-driving cars navigate the road. You have to show self-driving cars, this is a car, this is a tree, this is a bike, this is a pedestrian, this is how you avoid all of them, these are the lane markings, this is what the lane markings mean. And they’re humans that do that.

And it just so happened in 2016, when this demand was rising, that Venezuela as a country was dealing with the worst peacetime economic crisis in 50 years. So the economy bottomed out. A huge population of highly educated workers with great access to internet suddenly were desperate to work at any price. And these became the three conditions that I call the “crisis playbook” in my book, that companies started using to scout out more workers that were extremely cheap for the AI industry.

And so the woman that I met in Colombia — she was working in a level of exploitation that was not based on the content she was looking at. She was labeling self-driving cars, and labeling retail platforms and things like that. The exploitation was structural to her job, in that she was logging into a platform every day and looking at a queue that automatically populated with tasks being sent to her from Global North companies. And most of the time the tasks didn’t appear, and when they did, she had to compete with other workers to claim the task first in order to do it at all.

And because there were so many Venezuelans in crisis, and so many of them were finding out about data annotation platforms, in the end there were more and more workers competing for smaller and smaller volumes of tasks. And so these tasks would come online and then disappear within seconds.

And so one day she was out on a walk when a task appeared in her queue, and she sprinted to her apartment to try and claim the task before it went away. But by the time she got back, it was too late. And after that she was like, I never went on a walk during the weekday again. And on the weekends, which she discovered is less likely for companies to post tasks, she would only allow herself a 30-minute walk break, because she was too afraid of that happening again.

Karen Hao: It completely controlled her life. And she would turn it on to max volume in the middle of the night, because sometimes tasks would arrive in the middle of the night, and if the alarm rang she would wake up, sprint to her computer, claim the task, and then start tasking at like 3 a.m.

And she had chronic illness. One of the reasons she was tethered to her apartment doing this online work in the first place was not just because she was a refugee, but also because she had severe diabetes. And so she was tethered to her home because she had to inject herself with insulin like five times a day, and it was this really complicated regime that didn’t allow her to commute to a regular office, have a regular job. So she was doing all this extremely disruptive, dysregulating work on top of just trying to manage extreme, severe diabetes.

And the way that I think about it is the full supply chain of AI development: you have a bunch of resources that these companies need to develop their technologies — data, land, energy, water — and then you have a bunch of spaces that these companies need access to to deploy their technologies — schools, hospitals, offices, government agencies.
